Mary.text: St. Jerome translated it as "drop of the sea"; a scribal error turned that into "star of the sea", Stella Maris.
Mary.evidence: St. Jerome (writing c. 390), following Eusebius of Caesarea, translates the name as "drop of the sea" (stilla maris in Latin) ... This translation was subsequently rendered stella maris ("star of the sea") due to scribal error, whence Our Lady's title Star of the Sea.

Patricia.text: It peaked at third for newborn girls from 1937 to 1943; by 2016 it had slid to 745th.
Patricia.evidence: According to the US Social Security Administration records, the use of the name for newborns peaked at #3 from 1937 to 1943 in the United States, after which it dropped in popularity, sliding to #745 in 2016.

Jennifer.text: It's the Cornish form of Guinevere, and was rare elsewhere until George Bernard Shaw used it in The Doctor's Dilemma.
Jennifer.evidence: Jennifer ... is a feminine given name, the Cornish form of Guinevere ... Before 1906, the name was fairly uncommon elsewhere in English-speaking countries, but it gained some recognition after George Bernard Shaw used it for the main female character in The Doctor's Dilemma.

Linda.text: The 1946 song "Linda" was named after the songwriter's lawyer's one-year-old daughter: the future Linda McCartney.
Linda.evidence: "Linda" is a popular song written and published in 1946 by Jack Lawrence. ... The song was written in 1942 when Lawrence was in the service during World War II, taking its name from the then one-year-old daughter of his attorney, Lee Eastman. (His daughter was Linda Eastman McCartney, future first wife of the Beatle Paul McCartney.)

Elizabeth.text: It comes from the Hebrew Elisheva, "My God is an oath", the name of Aaron's wife in the Bible.
Elizabeth.evidence: Elizabeth is a feminine given name, a variation of the Hebrew name Elisheva, meaning "My God is an oath" or "My God is abundance" ... "Elizabeth" appears in the Hebrew Bible as the name of Aaron's wife

Barbara.text: It's from the Greek for "foreign", and Saint Barbara, locked in a tower by her father, may have inspired Rapunzel.
Barbara.evidence: They are the feminine form of the Greek word barbaros meaning "stranger" or "foreign". In Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox tradition, Saint Barbara was imprisoned in a tower by her father. ... The story of Saint Barbara is said to have been an inspiration for the fairy tale Rapunzel

Susan.text: Ranked 96th in the 1880s, it fell out of the top 200 in the 1910s and 1920s, then climbed to third in the 1960s.
Susan.evidence: Rank table, Susan: 1880s 96, 1890s 123, 1900s 163, 1910s -, 1920s -, 1930s 117, 1940s 10, 1950s 4, 1960s 3 (a dash means not in top 200 names). "Some (Susan, Emily, Amy, Amanda, and Emma) have risen and fallen and risen again in popularity."

Jessica.text: Its spelling first appears in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice; he may have taken it from "jess", a falconry strap.
Jessica.evidence: The oldest written record of the name with its current spelling is found as the name of the Shakespearean character Jessica, from the play The Merchant of Venice. ... Alternately, Shakespeare might have derived the name from ... jess, a thin leather strap used to tether a bird such as a falcon in falconry.

Karen.text: In Armenia, Karen is a common boy's name, from one of the seven great noble houses of ancient Iran.
Karen.evidence: In Armenia Karen is a common masculine given name. The masculine given name Karen derived from the Parthian name of House of Karen (or Caren), one of the seven aristocratic families of ancient Iran.

Sarah.text: In Genesis, God renames Sarai as Sarah; most scholars think both forms mean "important woman".
Sarah.evidence: God gave Sarai the new name "Sarah", and blessed her. ... According to most modern scholars, both Sarah and Sarai come from the same root SRR, with both meaning "important woman".
